definition.text: A hierarchical, distributed naming service that translates human-readable domain names into the numeric IP addresses that computers use to find each other.

facts.text: DNS works like the phone book of the Internet: it translates human-friendly hostnames into IP addresses, so www.example.com translates to 93.184.216.34 (IPv4) and 2606:2800:220:1:248:1893:25c8:1946 (IPv6).

Responsibility for each domain goes to its authoritative name servers, and administrators can delegate subdomains to other name servers, which gives a distributed, fault-tolerant service designed to avoid one large central database.
Records can be updated quickly and transparently, so a service can change its network location while users keep using the same hostname.
The distributed nature of DNS lets it work efficiently while serving billions of hosts on the worldwide Internet.
A DNS name server stores the records for a domain and answers queries against its database, which is conventionally kept in a structured text file called a zone file.
DNS runs on port 53 over UDP and TCP; it originally used UDP, and reliability, security and privacy concerns later brought TCP and other transports.
DNS stores more than addresses: it has been extended to hold records such as DNSSEC records and, as a general-purpose database, spam blocklists.
The DNS mirrors administrative responsibility on the Internet: each subdomain is a zone of administrative autonomy delegated to a manager.

title: Domain name hierarchy
article: Domain Name System#Structure > Domain name space

definition.text: The DNS namespace is a tree whose nodes each have a label, and a full domain name is the labels from a node up to the root, joined by dots.

facts.text: The domain name space is a tree; each node or leaf has a label and zero or more resource records holding information about that domain name.
A domain name is its label joined by a dot to the name of its parent node on the right, and the rightmost label is the top-level domain: www.example.com belongs to the TLD com.
The hierarchy descends from right to left, each label naming a subdivision of the domain to its right, so www is a subdomain of example.com; the tree may have up to 127 levels.
The tree divides into zones beginning at the root zone, and a zone may contain as many domains and subdomains as its manager chooses.
TLDs come in several types, for example generic TLDs (.com, .org), country code TLDs (.us) and a test TLD (.test).
A label may contain zero to 63 characters and the null label is reserved for the root; a full name may not exceed 253 characters in its textual form.
Hostname labels follow the LDH rule (letters, digits, hyphen), cannot start or end with a hyphen, and are interpreted case-independently.
Applications such as web browsers use IDNA to map Unicode strings into the valid DNS character set with Punycode, which lets names appear in native alphabets.

definition.text: Delegation is the mechanism that assigns responsibility for different parts of the DNS namespace to different name servers.

facts.text: Responsibility for a zone can be divided by creating additional zones; authority over the new zone is delegated to a designated name server and the parent zone stops being authoritative for it.
Each public domain under the TLDs is delegated through an NS record in the parent domain that points to the DNS names of the name servers of the child domain.
Name servers in a delegation are identified by name rather than address, so a resolver must issue another DNS request to find the address of the server it was referred to.
If the delegated name server is a subdomain of the domain it serves, there is a circular dependency, and the delegating server must supply the server's IP addresses as glue.
A glue record combines a name server and an IP address; the delegating server returns glue in the additional section of its response and the delegation in the authority section.

For example, resolving www.example.org needs ns1.example.org, which needs example.org first; the org TLD name server breaks the loop by including address records for ns1.example.org along with the delegation.

title: Authoritative name server
article: Domain Name System#Structure > Name servers > Authoritative name server

definition.text: A name server that answers DNS queries only from data configured by an original source, such as the domain administrator, rather than from a cache of another server's answers.

facts.text: Each domain has at least one authoritative server that publishes information about the domain and about the name servers of any domains subordinate to it.
An authoritative server is either primary, holding the original copies of all zone records, or secondary, which keeps an identical copy through an automatic updating mechanism in the DNS protocol.
A zone's set of authoritative name servers is stored in the parent zone as NS records; RFC 1034 requires every zone to be available on at least two servers so it survives host or link failure.
An authoritative server marks its answers as definitive by setting the Authoritative Answer (AA) bit; a server named as authoritative for a domain it has no data for causes a lame delegation.
The authoritative name server is usually the resolver's last stop: it holds information specific to its domain, such as the A record, and returns NXDOMAIN if it cannot find the domain.
Dynamic DNS updates use the UPDATE opcode to add or remove records in the zone database on an authoritative server, for example to register network clients when they boot.
The authoritative name server provides the actual answer to a DNS query, and you register authoritative name servers with a domain name registrar.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

title: DNS lookup process
article: Domain Name System#Operation > Address resolution mechanism

definition.text: To resolve a name, a resolver asks a root server, then a top-level domain server, then the domain's authoritative server, following referrals until it receives an authoritative answer.

facts.text: Resolvers find the responsible servers through queries that begin with the rightmost (top-level) label, and each host is configured with hints, an initial cache of the known addresses of the root name servers.
With no cached records, resolution starts at a root server; roots usually do not answer directly but refer the resolver onward, so a query for www.wikipedia.org is referred to the org servers.
The resolver queries the servers it was referred to and repeats this iteratively until it receives an authoritative answer.

The three levels of DNS servers are the root name servers, which hold the addresses of TLD name servers; the TLD servers, which hold the addresses of authoritative servers; and the authoritative servers, which give the actual answer.
For google.com, the browser hands the name to the DNS resolver, which asks a root server for the .com TLD server, asks that server for the domain's authoritative name server, and queries it.
The authoritative name server returns the IP address for google.com to the resolver, which passes it back to the web browser.
There are 13 logical root name servers, and thirteen groups of root servers exist with additional copies distributed worldwide by anycast addressing.

Starting every lookup at the root would put a large burden on the root servers, so caching in DNS servers off-loads them and roots handle only a small fraction of all requests; lookups average 20-120 milliseconds, according to YSlow.

definition.text: The client side of DNS, which initiates and sequences the queries that end in a full resolution, such as turning a domain name into an IP address.

facts.text: A resolver is a program that sits between user programs and name servers, on the same machine as the program it serves; because it may consult several servers or its cache, it can take from milliseconds to several seconds.

Applications ask the resolver in the local operating system, which answers from its cache of recent lookups if it can and otherwise queries designated DNS servers, usually the ISP's, set up manually or through DHCP.
The resolver caches the result for future use and hands it back to the software that asked.

A recursive resolver is the first stop in a DNS query and a middleman between client and name servers: it answers from cache or asks a root, then a TLD, then an authoritative name server, and replies to the client.

Caching DNS servers store results for the record's time-to-live and usually also implement recursion from the root down; ISPs typically provide such servers, and many home routers implement DNS caches and recursion.
With only authoritative servers operating, every query would have to start with recursive queries at the root zone and each user system would need resolver software capable of recursion.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

definition.text: Resolvers are classified by query method: in a recursive query a server resolves the name fully on the client's behalf, in an iterative query the client follows referrals, and a non-recursive query needs no further rounds.

facts.text: Resolvers are classified by query method as recursive, non-recursive or iterative, and a single resolution may combine them.

In a recursive query the client asks one server, which answers completely by querying other name servers as needed, or returns an error; a stub resolver on a home router typically does this against the ISP's server.

In an iterative query the resolver asks a chain of servers, each referring it to the next until one can fully resolve the request: for www.example.com, a root server, then a com server, then an example.com server.
In a non-recursive query the server already has the answer, from its cache or as an authoritative server, or returns a partial result, so no further rounds of queries are needed.

Typically a client sends a recursive query to a caching recursive server, which issues non-recursive queries and returns a single answer; use of recursion is negotiated with bits in the query headers.

RFC 1034 requires name servers to implement the iterative approach, which suits datagram access, and allows the recursive approach as an option, so DNS servers are not required to support recursive queries.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

title: DNS caching and TTL

definition.text: DNS reduces query load by caching resolution results locally or on intermediary resolvers, each result carrying a time to live (TTL) that says how long it stays valid.

facts.text: A key goal of the resolver is to remove network delay and name server load from most requests by answering from its cache, and caches shared by many processes, users or machines are more efficient than unshared ones.

The authoritative server's administrator sets the TTL, from a few seconds to several days or weeks; RFC 1912 gives 1 to 5 days as typical and 1 to 2 weeks for rarely changing records; some resolvers override TTLs.
A cached record keeps its TTL, which the server counts down every second; at zero the record is purged and the next query for it must start the resolution process again.

Because caching is distributed, record changes do not propagate immediately but only after all caches expire and refresh after the TTL; TTLs can be lowered before a change, at the cost of more network traffic.
RFC 1034 makes negative caching an optional service: a name error can be distributed with a TTL, and the SOA record's MINIMUM field limits how long the negative result may be cached.
Wikipedia describes the negative-answer TTL as set from the SOA's minimum field together with the SOA's own TTL, which reflects later practice than RFC 1034's MINIMUM-only rule.
Caching in DNS servers keeps the root name servers involved in only a small fraction of all requests.
Web browsers often keep an internal DNS cache, typically for around one minute, which obscures the history of the data and makes DNS issues harder to debug; some large ISPs even disobey TTLs.

notes: RFC 1034 (1987) says the SOA MINIMUM field alone sets the negative-caching time; Wikipedia says the SOA minimum and the SOA's own TTL are used (later practice). Treated as a version difference, not a conflict.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

definition.text: Resource records are the information elements of the DNS database, each with a type, a time to live, a class and type-specific data.

facts.text: On the wire every record has NAME, TYPE, CLASS, TTL, RDLENGTH and RDATA fields; the TTL counts the seconds the record stays valid, up to a maximum of 2^31 minus 1, about 68 years.

TYPE gives the data's format and use, RDATA holds the type-specific data such as an address or an MX priority and hostname, and CLASS is IN for ordinary Internet records, each class being an independent name space.
Records of the same type form a resource record set (RRset) with no special ordering; resolvers return the whole set, though servers may use round-robin ordering to balance load.
Wildcard records have names starting with the asterisk label and generate records within a single zone by substituting whole labels with matching components of the query name.

definition.text: The record types of DNS name the kinds of information a domain publishes, such as addresses (A, AAAA), aliases (CNAME), mail servers (MX), name servers (NS), reverse pointers (PTR), services (SRV) and text (TXT).

facts.text: An A record maps a domain name to an IPv4 address, and an AAAA record does the same for an IPv6 address; both are essential for turning domain names into IP addresses.

A CNAME record aliases one domain name to another, often pointing subdomains at the main domain while keeping the actual domain name hidden; it forwards to the other name and does not itself provide an IP address.
An MX record directs email traffic to the correct mail server, which also adds a layer of fault tolerance and load distribution for mail delivery.
An NS record specifies the authoritative DNS servers for a domain and directs queries to the correct servers for further lookups.
A PTR record provides reverse DNS lookup by mapping an IP address back to a domain name, and is commonly used to verify the authenticity of a server.
An SRV record specifies a host and port for services such as VoIP and is used together with A records.
A TXT record lets the administrator attach human-readable text to a domain, for example verification records such as SPF for email security.
The SOA (start of authority) record stores administrative information about a domain and is among the most common types in the DNS database, alongside A, AAAA, MX, NS, PTR and CNAME.

definition.text: A reverse DNS lookup queries the DNS for the domain names tied to an IP address that is already known.

facts.text: Addresses are stored as PTR records under the infrastructure TLD arpa, in-addr.arpa for IPv4 and ip6.arpa for IPv6, with the address written in reverse order: 208.80.152.2 becomes 2.152.80.208.in-addr.arpa.

The client converts the address into that name and queries for a PTR record, following the delegation chain as for any DNS query; with no PTR record the lookup cannot resolve, and several names may share one IP address.
Email servers commonly use reverse lookups to check that a message came from a valid server, and many reject messages from servers that do not support reverse lookups.

Reverse lookups are not universally adopted because they are not critical to the normal function of the Internet; RFC 1034 says inverse queries are not an acceptable way to map addresses to host names and IN-ADDR.ARPA should be used.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

definition.text: DNS can spread traffic and add fault tolerance because hostnames and IP addresses need not match one to one: one name can resolve to many addresses and different users can get different answers.

facts.text: A single hostname can resolve to many IP addresses to give fault tolerance and load distribution across server instances in an enterprise or across the Internet.

Distributed services such as cloud services and CDNs translate a domain name to the IP address of a server near the user, because different users can receive different answers for the same name at the same time.
Assigning nearby servers through DNS is key to faster and more reliable Internet responses and is widely used by most major Internet services.
Servers may use round-robin ordering of a record set to balance load, and an MX record can provide an extra layer of fault tolerance and load distribution for mail.
Multiple hostnames can map to a single IP address for virtual hosting; the HTTP Host header then tells the server which name was requested, allowing name-based virtual hosting.

definition.text: DNS queries and responses share one message format: a header followed by question, answer, authority and additional sections.

facts.text: The header holds Identification, Flags and the counts of questions, answers, authority records and additional records, each field 16 bits long; the identification field matches responses to queries.
Header flags tell whether the message is a query or reply (QR), whether the answer is authoritative (AA), whether it was truncated (TC), and whether recursion is desired (RD) or available (RA).
The response code RCODE can be NOERROR (0), FORMERR (1, format error), SERVFAIL (2) or NXDOMAIN (3, nonexistent domain).
The question section, usually one record, holds a NAME, TYPE and CLASS, and each label of the name is prefixed by its length with the name ending in a zero octet for the root.

definition.text: DNS queries travel over classic UDP and TCP on port 53 or over encrypted transports such as DNS over TLS, DNS over HTTPS, DNS over QUIC and DNSCrypt.

facts.text: Classic DNS sends a clear-text request in a single UDP packet to port 53 and gets a clear-text reply in a single UDP packet; with EDNS support, answers longer than 512 bytes may use larger UDP packets.

UDP is limited by its lack of transport-layer encryption, authentication, reliable delivery and message length; RFC 1123 (1989) added optional TCP, which allows longer responses, reliable delivery and reuse of long-lived connections.
UDP suits simple query-response protocols such as DNS, and TCP's complexity can be a problem for servers answering simple requests from huge numbers of clients.
DNS over TLS (2016) protects the entire connection with TLS on TCP port 853; RFC 7858 supports opportunistic and authenticated encryption but did not make server or client authentication mandatory.
DNS over HTTPS (2018) tunnels queries over HTTPS on TCP port 443, so it looks like web traffic, though the two are easily told apart without proper padding.
DNS over QUIC (RFC 9250, 2022) has privacy properties similar to DoT and latency characteristics similar to classic DNS over UDP; it is not the same as DNS over HTTP/3.
DNSCrypt (2011), developed outside the IETF, has clients encrypt query payloads with servers' public keys published in the DNS, and uses TCP or UDP port 443.

title: DNS security issues

definition.text: DNS was designed without strong security, so responses can be forged or abused, and extensions such as DNSSEC and TSIG were added to authenticate them.

facts.text: In DNS cache poisoning, data is fed to caching resolvers as though from an authoritative server, polluting the cache with false information and long TTLs, so legitimate requests may be redirected to malicious hosts.

DNS responses traditionally carry no cryptographic signature; DNSSEC adds signed responses, while TSIG adds authentication between trusted peers and is commonly used to authorize zone transfers and dynamic updates.
Because DNS is often seen as innocuous and passes firewalls, it can leak from private connections or carry malware commands in TXT records, as in DNSMessenger, and be used to exfiltrate data.
Lookalike names such as paypal.com and paypa1.com can be indistinguishable in some fonts, an IDN homograph attack that is occasionally exploited in phishing.

notes: Early-design note dropped: security was not a design concern while the early network was closed (93058dabf211, ed25638cc381).

title: DNS privacy
article: Domain Name System#Privacy and tracking issues

definition.text: Because DNS has no confidentiality controls, queries are exposed, and the ways of protecting them are themselves argued over.

facts.text: Designed as a public, heavily cached database, DNS has no confidentiality controls: unencrypted queries and responses allow sniffing, hijacking, cache poisoning and man-in-the-middle attacks.

Defenses include VPNs, which move resolution to the VPN operator, Tor, and proxies or public DNS servers, which move resolution to a trusted third party; some public servers support DoH, DoT and DNSCrypt.
Solutions that stop the local network operator inspecting DNS are criticized for thwarting corporate security policies and Internet censorship.
Public DNS servers are criticized for centralizing control of resolution in the few large companies that can afford to run public resolvers.

contested_note: Encrypted and public DNS are criticized for undermining network security policies and for centralizing resolution.

definition.text: The right to use a domain name is delegated by registrars, which are accredited by ICANN or similar organizations, while a registry runs the database of names for each TLD.

facts.text: A registrant is the person or organization that asked for the registration; registrants are customers of the registrar, in some cases through additional subcontracting of resellers.
A registry operates the database of names within its authoritative zone, receives registration information from accredited registrars and publishes it using the WHOIS protocol.
In the registry-registrar model used by COM, NET and ORG, the registry manages only the domain name database and its relationship with the many registrars.
Most gTLD registries have used a thick registry approach since about 2001, keeping WHOIS data centrally; COM and NET use a thin model in which the registry holds only basic WHOIS data.

definition.text: DNS replaced the single centrally maintained HOSTS.TXT file of ARPANET host names, which became slow and unwieldy as the network grew.

facts.text: Before DNS, one file, HOSTS.TXT, maintained by the Network Information Center, mapped host names to the numerical addresses of ARPANET computers, and all hosts FTPed it.
The bandwidth consumed distributing each new version was proportional to the square of the number of hosts, and the outgoing FTP load on the NIC host was considerable.
Local organizations administered their own names and addresses but had to wait for the NIC to change HOSTS.TXT before changes became visible, and they also wanted local structure in the name space.

By the early 1980s a single centralized host table had become slow and unwieldy; Paul Mockapetris created DNS in 1983, and RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 superseded the original specifications in November 1987.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

definition.text: DNS was designed to give one consistent name space that is distributed and cached, useful for many applications, and independent of any one network, protocol or host type.

facts.text: The primary goal is a consistent name space, with names that need not contain network identifiers, addresses or routes; the database must be distributed, with local caching, rather than collected as one consistent copy.

Creating and deleting names should be distributed too, and where there are trade-offs between the cost of acquiring data, update speed and cache accuracy, the data's source should control the trade-off.
The facility should serve many applications, so all data is tagged with a type and a class, letting queries target one type and the same name space carry different protocol families' address formats.

Name server transactions should not depend on the transport, whether datagrams for queries or virtual circuits where reliability matters, and the system should suit both personal computers and large timeshared hosts.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

definition.text: DNS favors availability of name data over instant consistency: updates spread gradually, and cached copies expire on timers that the data's owner sets.

facts.text: RFC 1034 treats access to information as more critical than instantaneous updates or consistency guarantees, so updates percolate out through the users of the system rather than reaching every copy at once.
When updates are unavailable because of network or host failure, the usual course is to believe old information while continuing efforts to update it.
Copies are distributed with timeouts for refreshing: the distributor sets the timeout, the recipient performs the refresh, very short intervals can be specified, and the owner can prohibit copies.
Most data changes very slowly, such as mailbox bindings and host addresses, but the system must also handle subsets that change on the order of seconds or minutes.
Each organization responsible for a set of domains provides redundant name servers, and every zone must be available on at least two servers so it stays available despite host or link failure.
All data originates in master files that local administrators update; a local name server reads them and serves them to users through resolvers.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

title: DNS components
article: rfc>1034#2. INTRODUCTION > 2.4. Elements of the DNS

definition.text: DNS has three major components: the domain name space with its resource records, name servers that hold the data, and resolvers that extract it for clients.

facts.text: A name server has complete information about a subset of the space, for which it is the authority, plus pointers to other servers; authoritative information is organized into zones distributed to redundant servers.

Resolvers extract information from name servers for client requests, answering directly or following referrals; a resolver is typically a system routine, so no protocol is needed between it and the user program.
To the user DNS is a call to a local resolver over one tree; to the resolver, an unknown number of name servers; to a name server, zones it must refresh from master copies while answering queries.
Implementations may couple these functions for performance: a resolver on the same machine as a name server might share one database of the server's zones and the resolver's cache.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

title: DNS zone
article: rfc>1034#4. NAME SERVERS > 4.2. How the database is divided into zones

definition.text: A zone is a connected region of the name space, bounded by cuts where authority is handed on, for which a set of name servers holds the authoritative data.

facts.text: Cuts can be made between any two adjacent nodes, and each group of connected name space then forms a separate zone that is authoritative for all names in that region.

A DNS zone is a distinct part of the name space delegated to a person, organization or company that maintains it, and it is also an administrative unit giving granular control of components such as authoritative name servers.

An organization that controls a zone can change its data unilaterally, grow new tree sections, delete nodes or delegate subzones, and larger organizations can nest delegations to match their substructure.

A zone's data has four parts: authoritative data for all its nodes, data for its top node, data describing delegated subzones, and data giving access to the subzones' name servers, all expressed as resource records.

The top node carries NS records listing every server for the zone and a single SOA record holding zone management parameters, while NS records at the bottom cuts name the subzones' servers and are not authoritative data of this zone.
NS records name servers but give no addresses, so a zone also holds glue records, address records for servers whose names lie below the cut, used only in referral responses.

To take over a domain, an organization finds the parent zone, gets its owners to agree to the delegation, shows redundant name server support, and has the delegation NS and glue records added to the parent zone.
A zone's servers need not sit inside the zone's own domain, and spreading them widely can make a zone more accessible: one name server for the UK domain is in the US, saving transatlantic bandwidth.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

title: DNS zone transfer
article: rfc>1034#4. NAME SERVERS > 4.3. Name server internals > 4.3.5. Zone maintenance and transfers

definition.text: A zone transfer is how a secondary name server polls its primary and copies a changed zone, so every authoritative server for a zone serves the same data.

facts.text: Changes are made at the primary, typically by editing a master file and then signalling the server to load it; the preferred way to spread them is the DNS protocol's zone transfer, not FTP or ad hoc procedures.

Secondary servers check for changes at a selectable interval by comparing the SERIAL field of the zone's SOA record, which must advance whenever the zone changes so that the more recent of two copies can be told apart.

The SOA parameters REFRESH, RETRY and EXPIRE control polling: a secondary waits REFRESH seconds between checks, retries every RETRY seconds if a check cannot complete, and after EXPIRE seconds without one must discard its copy as obsolete.
The check is a simple query to the primary for the zone's SOA record; if the serial equals the secondary's, nothing changed and the REFRESH wait restarts.
When the serial shows a change, the secondary requests a zone transfer with an AXFR request, answered by a stream of messages that carry every record of the zone and let the secondary build its copy.
Because accuracy is essential, AXFR requests must use TCP or another reliable protocol.
Secondaries may also run these operations against other secondaries, which helps when the primary is down or an intermediate secondary has better network access than the primary.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

title: Stub resolver
article: rfc>1034#5. RESOLVERS > 5.3. Resolver internals > 5.3.1. Stub resolvers

definition.text: A stub resolver moves the resolution work off the local machine and into a name server that supports recursive queries, keeping only a list of such servers.

facts.text: Moving resolution into a recursive name server gives a PC that lacks the resources to resolve names an easy way to use DNS, and can centralize the cache for a whole local network or organization.
The stub needs only a configured list of name server addresses that will perform recursive requests, and a name server is free to refuse recursive service to any or all clients.
A simple stub resolver on a home router typically makes a recursive query to the DNS server run by the user's ISP.

The drawbacks are that recursive requests take arbitrary time, so the stub struggles to tune retransmissions for lost UDP packets and dead servers, and the server can be overloaded if it treats retransmissions as new requests.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

definition.text: RFC 1034's resolver algorithm answers from local data if it can and otherwise finds the best servers, queries them and analyzes each response.

facts.text: The resolver's four steps are: look for the answer in local information and return it if found; find the best servers to ask; send them queries until one responds; analyze the response.

An answer or name error is cached and returned; a better delegation is cached and the server search repeats; a CNAME is cached and the search restarts at the canonical name; a failed server is dropped and the next tried.

To pick servers it looks for known NS records at the name, then its parent, up toward the root; with none it uses a configured safety belt, usually two root servers and two servers for its own domain.

Authoritative data is preferred to cached data, and the resolver should bound its work so a loop cannot start even with misconfigured data, avoid unnecessary transmissions, and parse responses very suspiciously.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

title: CNAME records and aliases
article: rfc>1034#3. DOMAIN NAME SPACE and RESOURCE RECORDS > 3.6. Resource Records > 3.6.2. Aliases and canonical names

definition.text: A CNAME record marks its owner name as an alias and names the canonical (primary) name that holds the real data.

facts.text: A resource often has several names: one canonical (primary) name and aliases. A CNAME record marks its owner name as an alias and gives the canonical name, but provides no IP address itself.
If a node has a CNAME record it should hold no other data, so an alias and its canonical name cannot differ and a cached CNAME can be used without asking an authoritative server about other types.

A server that finds a CNAME instead of the wanted record includes it in the response and restarts the query at the canonical name, except for CNAME-type queries; the resolver does a whole new lookup for that name.
Records that point at another name should use the primary name, not an alias, to avoid extra indirection; software should follow CNAME chains and signal CNAME loops as an error.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

title: DNS standard queries
article: rfc>1034#3. DOMAIN NAME SPACE and RESOURCE RECORDS > 3.7. Queries > 3.7.1. Standard queries

definition.text: A standard query names a domain (QNAME), a record type (QTYPE) and a class (QCLASS) and asks a name server for the matching records.

facts.text: Standard queries are the vast majority of DNS queries, and they travel in UDP datagrams or over TCP connections.
A server may add records that point toward a name server holding the data or that help interpret the answer: a query for the MX records of ISI.EDU also returns the mail exchangers' addresses.

Name servers may support inverse queries that map a resource to the domain names having it, but these are mainly for debugging and database maintenance, are not guaranteed complete, and their results should never be cached.
Inverse queries are not an acceptable way to map host addresses to host names; the IN-ADDR.ARPA domain is used instead.

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain names - concepts and facilities

title: Root and TLD name servers

definition.text: Root name servers direct resolvers to the right top-level domain servers, and TLD name servers hold the information for every domain under one extension such as .com.

facts.text: A root server answers requests for records in the root zone and otherwise directs the resolver to the TLD name servers for the domain's extension, such as .com, .net or .org.
The root zone file, about 2 MB, lists the authoritative servers for all TLDs; a root server answers with a referral to the right TLD servers or says that no such TLD exists.
Only thirteen root server addresses exist because the original DNS limits UDP packets to 512 bytes; IPv6 addresses need more, which the EDNS0 extension allows.

The root system is far more than 13 machines: each operator runs redundant equipment in many locations using anycast addressing, so there are about 1954 instances for better performance and fault tolerance.

A resolver bootstraps from hints, a small root.hints file of root server addresses, which breaks the circular need to know a root server's address before resolving anything; caching keeps root lookups infrequent.
A TLD name server maintains information for all domain names sharing an extension, the part after the last dot, and answers with the address of the domain's authoritative name server.
TLD servers fall into two main groups: generic TLDs such as .com, .org, .net, .edu and .gov, and country code TLDs such as .uk, .us, .ru and .jp.
Each TLD is maintained and serviced technically by an administrative organization that operates a registry.

definition.text: A subdomain is an extra part added to a main domain name, commonly used to split a website into logical sections.

facts.text: Multiple subdomains or child domains can be created on a main domain, and they are commonly used to logically separate a website into sections.
In blog.example.com, blog is the subdomain, example is the primary domain and .com is the top-level domain; support.example.com and careers.example.com are similar examples.
Each subdomain can be delegated to its own manager as a zone of administrative autonomy.

definition.text: DNSSEC is a suite of IETF extensions that secures DNS data by adding digital signatures, so resolvers can detect forged or altered answers.

facts.text: The original DNS design had no security features; DNSSEC adds them while keeping backward compatibility, to stop applications accepting forged or manipulated DNS data such as that created by DNS cache poisoning.
DNSSEC gives cryptographic authentication of data, authenticated denial of existence and data integrity, but not availability or confidentiality: responses are authenticated but not encrypted.

All answers from a DNSSEC-protected zone are signed, so a resolver can check that the data is unmodified and complete as published by the zone owner; any DNS data can be protected, such as TXT and MX records.
DNSSEC signs record sets with public-key cryptography: each answer carries an RRSIG record, a signature checked with the public key found in a DNSKEY record.
A DS record placed in the parent zone refers to a DNSKEY record in the delegated zone, and NSEC or NSEC3 records give cryptographic evidence that a record does not exist.

A security-aware resolver sets the DO flag in its query; the flag lives in the EDNS extended flags, so all DNSSEC transactions must support EDNS, which also allows the much larger packets DNSSEC needs.
DNSSEC does not protect directly against DoS attacks and cannot protect against false assumptions about names; other standards secure bulk transfers between servers such as zone transfers.

Deployment has been hampered by the need for a backward-compatible standard that scales, preventing zone enumeration, rolling out across many servers and resolvers, disagreement over root key ownership, and perceived complexity.

title: DNSSEC chain of trust
article: Domain Name System Security Extensions#Operation > Trust anchors and authentication chains

definition.text: DNSSEC validation follows a chain of linked DS and DNSKEY records from a trust anchor, usually the DNS root key, down to the zone that signed the answer.

facts.text: An answer can be proved correct only if at least one key or DS record is known to be correct from a source other than DNS; these starting points are trust anchors, typically supplied with the operating system.
An authentication chain is a series of linked DS and DNSKEY records from a trust anchor to the domain's authoritative server; without a complete chain, an answer cannot be securely authenticated.
A DS record in a parent zone verifies a DNSKEY record in a subdomain, which can hold further DS records to verify deeper subdomains.

To validate www.example.com, a resolver ideally starts with the DS and DNSKEY at the root, uses the root's DS for com to verify com's DNSKEY, then example.com's DS and DNSKEY, and finally the RRSIG on the answer.

A DS record in the parent with no RRSIG in the reply signals something wrong: a man in the middle stripping the DNSSEC data, a broken security-oblivious server along the path, or a configuration error.
If a signed zone sits below a parent or the root that is not signed, it forms an island of security that must be validated another way, and trust anchors must still be configured for it.
DNSSEC was deployed at the root on July 15, 2010; the root trust anchor can then validate any zone with a complete chain of trust from the root.

A stub resolver forwards the query to a recursive server and uses the Authenticated Data (AD) bit as a hint that signatures were validated, or can set the Checking Disabled (CD) bit to validate itself.

title: DNSSEC key management
article: Domain Name System Security Extensions#Operation > Key management

definition.text: DNSSEC key management covers the key signing and zone signing keys, how they are rolled over, and how signature validity is limited in time.

facts.text: Key signing keys (KSK) sign the DNSKEY records that hold zone signing keys (ZSK), which sign the other records; ZSKs can be switched more easily and can be shorter, which shrinks RRSIG and DNSKEY records.
A new KSK needs its DS record transferred to the parent zone; DS records hold a message digest of the KSK rather than the full key, which keeps them small for very large zones such as com.

A key rollover first publishes the new keys in new DNSKEY records beside the old ones, uses them once cached old keys have expired by TTL, then deletes the old DNSKEY records after caches of old signatures expire.

RRSIG records carry absolute timestamps that limit replay, so resolver clocks must be roughly in sync, and a zone must be re-signed and redistributed regularly or validating resolvers will reject its signatures.

title: DNSSEC denial of existence
article: Domain Name System Security Extensions#Authenticating NXDOMAIN responses and NSEC

definition.text: DNSSEC proves that a name does not exist by returning signed NSEC or NSEC3 records that show where a gap in the zone lies.

facts.text: Proving a name is absent means signing the answer to every query for a non-existent name, which is hard because DNSSEC was designed for offline signing, and it is impossible to pre-generate a response to every hostname.

NSEC records link each pair of names in a zone, so a query for k.example.com is answered with an NSEC saying nothing exists between a.example.com and z.example.com; this exposes real names and so allows zone enumeration.

NSEC3 hashes the names instead of listing them, but GPUs and dedicated hardware let NSEC3 responses be brute-forced cheaply with offline dictionary attacks; NSEC5 has been proposed as a further alternative.
Online signing servers return a 'white lie', an NSEC whose names lexically surround the requested name, such as one proving nothing exists between j.example.com and l.example.com for k.example.com.

definition.text: DNS cache poisoning, also called DNS spoofing, introduces corrupt data into a resolver's cache so that it returns a wrong answer, such as an attacker's IP address.

facts.text: When a DNS server caches a false translation it is poisoned and supplies the false data to clients, diverting their traffic to a computer the attacker chooses until the cache entry expires.
Poisoning a single DNS server affects the users it serves directly and those served by its downstream servers; the attacker exploits flaws in the DNS software.
A poisoned server can send users to a fake site for phishing or malware, and opens them to further risks such as denial of service and website hijacking.

In one variant a vulnerable server caches the extra A record for the target domain's name server from an answer about the attacker's own domain, letting the attacker resolve queries for the whole target domain.
Many attacks are prevented by being less trusting of other servers and ignoring any returned records not directly relevant to the query.

Source port randomization with cryptographically secure random numbers for the port and the 16-bit nonce greatly reduces the chance of a successful race attack, but NAT devices may rewrite source ports and remove the randomness.

DNSSEC counters cache poisoning with digital signatures that authenticate the data; where it is missing, end-to-end validation such as TLS certificate checks over HTTPS mitigates the attack at the transport or application layer.

title: Round-robin DNS

definition.text: Round-robin DNS spreads load across several servers by answering a name lookup with a list of IP addresses whose order is rotated on each response.

facts.text: The DNS holds several A records for one name, one per server hosting identical content; each response permutes the address list and clients normally try the first address, so successive users reach different servers.
Some resolvers reorder the list to favor numerically closer networks, which was standardized in RFC 3484 for IPv6; a Windows Vista bug on IPv4 once defeated the balancing.
Record caching in the DNS hierarchy and client-side address caching make round-robin DNS hard to manage, even though it is easy to implement.

It should not be relied on alone for availability: if a service at one listed address fails, DNS keeps handing out that address, though some desktop clients try alternates after a timeout of up to 30 seconds.

It only alternates the order of records and ignores transaction time, server load and congestion, so it suits many uniformly distributed connections to equal servers; otherwise it just distributes load.
Modified DNS servers can poll mirrored servers for availability and load and temporarily remove a server from the DNS pool until it reports being within specs again.

notes: Overlaps 'DNS load balancing' in the load-balancing chapter and 'DNS load distribution'; this one rests on the Round-robin DNS page (drawbacks, client behaviour, remedies).

definition.text: Anycast is an addressing and routing method in which one IP address is shared by servers in many locations, and traffic goes to the nearest one.

facts.text: Routers send packets for an anycast address to the location nearest the sender using their normal decision-making, typically the lowest number of BGP network hops.
In IPv4, hosts in different places share one IP address and each announces it by BGP; routers treat these as alternative routes and often pick the path with fewer hops, though some use other metrics.
IPv6 supports anycast explicitly in its addressing architecture, and the IPv4 method of advertising multiple routes for one address in BGP still works there, with the same use cases and limitations.

All Internet root name servers use anycast; many commercial DNS providers switched to it to increase query performance and redundancy and to balance load, and CDNs use it for DNS or HTTP connections to their distribution centers.

Early objections held that a long-lived TCP connection could be rerouted to another instance mid-connection; in practice this was not observed, measured failures from instance switches were below 0.017%, and CDN requests are short-lived and stateless.

Anycast gives automatic failover, usually with external heartbeat monitoring that withdraws a failed server's route announcement; if the announcement continues, the dead server becomes a black hole for nearby clients, the most serious failure mode.
The failure above hurts only clients closer to that server than to any other, not everyone; but the automation that withdraws routes can itself become a point of failure.

Anycast spreads DDoS traffic across the nearest nodes, but this depends on keeping the unicast addresses of nodes secret; and anyone whose route announcements are accepted can hijack anycast traffic, so announcements must be filtered.

definition.text: A top-level domain is the highest level of the DNS hierarchy below the root, the last label of any domain name, such as .com in www.example.com.

facts.text: TLD names are installed in the root zone; ICANN delegates management of most of them to specific organizations and operates IANA, which maintains the DNS root zone.

IANA distinguishes infrastructure (.arpa), generic (gTLD, three or more characters), generic restricted, sponsored (private sponsors set eligibility rules), country-code (ccTLD) and internationalized country-code TLDs.

ccTLDs are two letters and, with some historical exceptions, match the territory's two-letter ISO 3166 code; internationalized ones display in native script but use a Punycode-translated ASCII name in DNS.

.arpa was the first TLD, meant temporarily to ease the move from ARPANET host names, but after being used for reverse DNS it was found impractical to retire; now it serves infrastructure uses such as in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa.

The IETF reserves special-use names such as .example, .invalid, .localhost and .test (RFC 6761), .local for multicast DNS and .onion for Tor; they should not be used in production networks on the global DNS.

Made-up internal names can collide with new TLDs: ICANN rejected .home and .corp over conflicts with networks using them, and local domains such as test.dev collided with the .dev gTLD created in 2019.
A TLD is a DNS node with records of its own; dotless domains put A, AAAA or MX records on a TLD itself, a practice ICANN and the IAB have spoken out against as a security risk.

title: Time to live and hop limit

definition.text: Time to live (TTL), or hop limit, is a mechanism that limits the lifespan of data in a computer or network.

facts.text: A TTL may be a counter or timestamp attached to the data; once the count or time elapses the data is discarded or revalidated, which stops packets circulating forever in networks and manages caching in applications.
In IP, TTL is an 8-bit header field with a maximum of 255, set by the sender and reduced by every router; at zero the datagram is discarded and an ICMP Time Exceeded error goes back to the sender.
The IP field keeps an undeliverable datagram from circulating until the system is swamped; IPv4 defines it in seconds but in practice it falls by one per hop, so IPv6 renamed it hop limit.

In DNS, the authoritative server sets a TTL per record that tells caching resolvers how long to keep it; HTTP expresses lifetime as an expiry date through Expires, Cache-Control max-age and cookie expires.

notes: Network and DNS side of TTL (Wikipedia Time to live); 'Time to live' in the caching chapter is the cache-eviction TTL from ByteByteGo.

definition.text: Beyond A, AAAA, MX and NS, DNS defines many more record types for aliases, service discovery, certificates, DNSSEC and zone transfers.

facts.text: A DNAME record aliases a name and all its subnames, unlike CNAME, which aliases only the exact name; non-standard ALIAS or ANAME records synthesize A and AAAA records from a target so the bare domain can be aliased.

TXT began as human-readable text but since the early 1990s mostly carries machine-readable data such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC; SRV gives generalized service location for newer protocols instead of protocol-specific records like MX.

SVCB records give clients connection metadata such as supported protocols and alternative endpoints; the HTTPS record is a specialised SVCB that supplies HTTPS connection details up front, enabling Encrypted Client Hello and lower first-connection latency.
CAA constrains which certificate authorities may issue for a domain, TLSA associates a TLS server certificate or key with a name for DANE, and SSHFP publishes SSH host key fingerprints.
DNSSEC adds RRSIG for signatures, DNSKEY for the zone key, DS to identify a delegated zone's signing key, NSEC to prove a name does not exist, and NSEC3 to prove it without permitting zone walking.

Some types are used in the protocol itself: AXFR transfers a whole zone from primary to secondary, IXFR only the differences since a serial number, ANY returns all cached records, and OPT is the pseudo-record that supports EDNS.
Many early types are obsolete: MX replaced MD and MF, the WKS record is declared not to be relied upon, and HINFO is now repurposed for minimal answers to ANY queries.

definition.text: Split-horizon DNS lets a DNS implementation return different sets of DNS information for the same query, usually chosen by the source address of the request.

facts.text: It manages security and privacy by logically or physically separating DNS information for internal access, within a company say, from access over an unsecure public network such as the Internet.
A common case is a server with both a private LAN address and a public one: the same name resolves to either, depending on the client, so local clients reach it directly with lower latency.
It can use separate DNS server devices, several DNS server processes on one machine, or server software that selects zone records by the asker, a common feature of DNS server software.

Split-horizon gives different authoritative answers to one query while DNSSEC vouches for the data returned; these goals can cause confusion or false security alerts in poorly built networks, and research has recommended how to combine them.

definition.text: A domain name registrar is a company or office, accredited by a registry, that manages the reservation of Internet domain names for registrants.

facts.text: Registries contract with registrars to serve the public, and only a domain's designated registrar may modify or delete its information in the central registry database.

Registering a domain creates name server records in the parent zone pointing to the domain's authoritative servers, usually at least two; it does not imply DNS hosting, which most registrars offer as an optional service.
For DNSSEC, the registrar processes the owner's public key data and creates DS records for the parent zone; all new gTLD registries and registrars must support DNSSEC.

Changing registrar is a domain transfer under ICANN's transfer policy: the owner unlocks the domain and gets an authentication code from the old registrar, and the new registrar must obtain express authorization from the holder.
